question:
Patient note:
A 97-year-old retired civil engineer who spent five decades inspecting suspension bridges was brought to the outpatient perioperative medicine office this morning by his granddaughter after a urology team requested a comprehensive evaluation before scheduling image-guided brachytherapy for a recently discovered, organ-confined neoplasm of the prostate (transrectal biopsy three weeks earlier showed a single focus of acinar adenocarcinoma, Gleason score 3 + 4 = 7, magnetic-resonance imaging demonstrates capsular integrity and no nodal enlargement). The patient walked in with a polished mahogany cane he fashioned himself, greeting staff by name and accurately recalling the height of the center span of the last bridge he certified, testimony to an intact memory and sharp executive function; during history taking he recited his medication list without hesitation and named the current head of state, the clinic address, and today’s date. Musculoskeletal history is notable for long-standing seropositive rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed in his late sixties after an episode of painful morning stiffness in the metacarpophalangeal joints lasting more than an hour; he has taken methotrexate 10 mg weekly with folic acid for the past two decades, supplemented by low-dose prednisone bursts during winter flares, and follows regularly with rheumatology where the most recent Disease Activity Score was in the low range. Despite occasional ulnar deviation at the hands, he buttoned his shirt unassisted this morning and continues to spend afternoons carving chess pieces, describing only mild aching controlled by acetaminophen 500 mg as needed. Gastrointestinal review reveals a cratered duodenal lesion noted on esophagogastroduodenoscopy twelve years ago after dark, tarry stools; Helicobacter testing was positive and triple therapy administered, followed by eight weeks of pantoprazole until complete mucosal healing was documented. Since that episode he avoids non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, takes omeprazole 20 mg each dawn, and denies subsequent hematemesis, melena, coffee-ground emesis, or iron-deficiency anemia. He has never experienced jaundice, encephalopathy, fluid retention, or evidence of portal hypertension, and a right-upper-quadrant sonogram performed last month to evaluate biliary colic showed a smooth hepatic contour, patent hepatic and portal veins, and no ascites. Endocrine screening one week ago revealed fasting plasma glucose 96 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c 5.6 %, values that have remained stable for years without pharmacologic intervention; no clinician has labeled him diabetic, and he follows a breakfast routine of oatmeal and fruit and records his weekly weights on graph paper taped near the pantry. The patient firmly denies ever feeling crushing or squeezing substernal discomfort, radiation to jaw or arm, diaphoresis disproportionate to exertion, or syncope; he has never been hospitalized for myocardial infarction, and no clinician has informed him of coronary artery occlusion. He climbs the eight steps to his front porch carrying the morning newspaper without dyspnea and sleeps flat on a single pillow; he has also never received a diagnosis of congestive heart failure. Cardiologist notes from his annual wellness visit six months ago document a normal stress echocardiogram reaching 8 METS with no ischemic changes, preserved global systolic performance, and trivial aortic sclerosis appropriate for age. He similarly reports no episodes of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, ankle swelling, orthopnea, or unexplained weight gain; his daughter confirms that socks do not leave indents around the calves at bedtime. Vascular review is silent for calf cramping, hip or buttock pain on walking, cold extremities, or prior vascular interventions, and he has never been told he has peripheral arterial disease; pulses were graded 2 +/4 at all peripheral sites during today’s examination. Neurologic inquiry reveals no sudden unilateral weakness, slurred speech, facial droop, blurred vision, gait imbalance, seizure activity, or sensory loss, and he continues to beat his grandson at rapid-fire chess without oversight. He reports no prior cerebrovascular accident or transient ischemic attack and has never experienced paralysis or hemiplegia. Respiratory history is remarkable only for childhood pertussis; he never smoked, has no chronic cough or wheeze, has never carried a diagnosis of asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, or other chronic lung disorder, and lung fields were clear at the last chest radiograph obtained during prostate work-up. His medication list includes methotrexate and folic acid as noted, a daily 81-mg aspirin recommended by his primary practitioner for vascular prophylaxis, omeprazole nightly, acetaminophen as needed, and a multivitamin; he reports hives after a sulfonamide injection in the 1940s but no other drug allergies. He drinks a small glass of red wine with Sunday dinner, abstains from liquor, has never used illicit substances, and lives independently in a single-story cottage equipped with grab bars he installed himself. Family pedigree shows longevity—both parents surpassed ninety—with no early coronary events, cerebrovascular accidents, or cirrhotic complications. Vital signs recorded after five minutes of seated rest read temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 128/72 mm Hg in the right arm, heart rate 68 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97 % on room air; body mass index is 23 kg/m². Physical examination reveals an alert, pleasant gentleman sitting upright without distress; sclerae anicteric, oral mucosa moist. Carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, jugular venous pulsation rises 3 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, the apical impulse is nondisplaced in the fifth intercostal space mid-clavicular line, first and second heart sounds are crisp with a soft midsystolic murmur heard best at the right upper sternal border, no gallops, rubs, or peripheral edema. Lungs are resonant to percussion, breath sounds vesicular throughout, no wheezes or crackles. Abdomen is flat, bowel sounds normoactive, liver edge smooth and palpable 1 cm below the costal margin, no splenic tip, no tenderness, masses, or fluid wave; digital rectal examination deferred to urology. Extremities are warm with capillary refill under two seconds, radial, femoral, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses symmetrical; nail beds show no clubbing. Hands reveal mild ulnar deviation and Swan-neck deformities but no active synovitis. Neurologic testing finds orientation to person, place, time, and situation intact, clear and fluent speech, cranial nerves II–XII grossly normal, symmetric strength 5/5 in all extremities, deep tendon reflexes 2 +/4, intact light-touch and vibration sense to the great toes, and a steady tandem gait executed without aid. Recent laboratory data reviewed today: sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (estimated glomerular filtration rate 74 mL/min/1.73 m²), alanine aminotransferase 28 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 30 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 88 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, albumin 4.2 g/dL, international normalized ratio 1.0, hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, hematocrit 40 %, mean corpuscular volume 88 fL, white blood cell count 5.8 × 10⁹/L with a normal differential, and platelets 210 × 10⁹/L. Complete blood counts over the years have shown no leukocytosis, blasts, or cytopenias, and he has never been diagnosed with leukemia or other hematologic malignancies. He tested negative for human immunodeficiency virus during routine blood donor screening in his eighth decade and has had no exposures or illnesses suggestive of immunodeficiency. Electrocardiogram obtained in clinic shows normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats/min, PR interval 160 ms, QRS duration 90 ms, axis 20°, no pathologic Q waves, and nonspecific ST-T changes unchanged from prior tracings. He seeks counsel on peri-procedural management of methotrexate, gastric acid suppression around planned radiation, and confirmation that his cardiovascular and pulmonary status present no contraindication to the proposed curative therapy.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Use the age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), which adds age points to weighted comorbidities present at baseline.
- Age: <50 = 0, 50–59 = 1, 60–69 = 2, 70–79 = 3, and ≥80 = 4. At 97, he scores 4.
- Rheumatic disease: established rheumatoid arthritis = 1, even with low disease activity.
- Peptic ulcer disease: prior endoscopically documented duodenal ulcer = 1 despite subsequent healing.
- Solid tumor: current organ-confined prostate adenocarcinoma = 2 for nonmetastatic malignancy, not 6 for metastatic disease.
- Other CCI conditions: no MI, heart failure, peripheral or cerebrovascular disease, dementia, chronic lung disease, liver disease, diabetes, hemiplegia, moderate/severe renal disease, leukemia, lymphoma, or AIDS = 0 each.
Total = 4 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 8.
Final answer: 8
